title: Activity Selection (Interval Scheduling)
tagline: Always pick the earliest-finishing compatible activity — the canonical greedy proof.

intuition.analogy: Booking the most meetings in one room: each time, choose the meeting that ENDS soonest among those that don't clash. Finishing early frees the room as quickly as possible, leaving maximum room for the rest.
paragraphs: Interval scheduling asks for the maximum number of mutually non-overlapping intervals. The greedy rule is beautifully simple: sort by finish time and repeatedly take the next interval whose start is ≥ the last chosen finish.

Why earliest finish and not, say, shortest or earliest start? Because the earliest-finishing activity leaves the most remaining time for everything else — and any optimal solution can be 'exchanged' to start with it without losing count (the exchange argument).
This is the textbook example of when greedy is provably optimal, and it generalises to room allocation, CPU scheduling, and many 'maximise non-conflicting choices' problems.
intuition.keyIdea: Sort by finish time; greedily take each activity that starts after the last one finishes.

steps.title: Sort by finish time
steps.detail: Ascending end times so the soonest-finishing activity is always considered first.

steps.title: Greedily select
steps.detail: Track lastEnd = −∞. For each activity in order, if its start ≥ lastEnd, select it and update lastEnd to its finish.

steps.title: Count / collect
steps.detail: The number selected is the maximum possible non-overlapping set.

complexity.timeReason: Dominated by sorting; the scan is linear.
complexity.spaceReason: Constant extra space beyond the sort.

pitfalls: Sorting by start time (or duration) does NOT give the optimum — finish time is the correct key.
Define overlap consistently: does touching (start == end) count as a conflict? Adjust the ≥ vs >.
For weighted intervals, greedy fails — that needs DP.

dryRun.clickMoment: Picking (1,3) over the overlapping (1,8) is the crux — the short-but-early-finishing choice leaves room for (4,7) and (8,10), beating any greedy that grabbed the long interval.
